subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage: Darshan, you'll laugh, but for my whole first semester I called Amma every single night. From the hostel corridor, in my nightie, crying like a six-year-old. Especially in exam week. I'd ask her to tell me what she cooked, what the neighbour's cat did, anything. Once I made her sing the Bengali lullaby she used to sing when I was small. Twenty minutes of that, and then I could study. My roommate thought I was homesick-mad. Maybe I was. But Amma never said "grow up". She'd just say, "Urmila, eat something, then call me back if you need to." In second semester I noticed I was calling every other day. Now it's Sundays, mostly to tell her about the lab. I still ask for the lullaby before finals, though. One verse.

qa.q: What did Urmila once ask Amma to sing?
qa.a: The Bengali lullaby she used to sing when Urmila was small.

qa.q: Why did the nightly calls help Urmila during first-semester exams?
qa.a: Far from home and stressed, she needed to feel looked after, and Amma's voice and small stories soothed her enough to study.

qa.q: Which choice of Amma's helped Urmila grow steadier rather than more dependent?
qa.a: Never saying 'grow up', just comforting her and adding 'eat something, then call me back', which met the need while pointing her gently back to her own day.

qa.q: How might Urmila's roommate have seen the nightly calls?
qa.a: The roommate thought Urmila was 'homesick-mad', perhaps without realising the calls were helping her cope.

grounding: A first-year student recalls calling her mother in tears every night during exams, and how the calls eased as her confidence grew.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
I'm Darshan, and my room is next to Madhav's in Block C. Every evening at nine, I hear his voice through the wall, calling home. During exams it changes. He talks the way my little cousin talks, all "Papa, you tell me" and "Papa, don't cut the call yet". Twice I've heard him crying. Once he asked his father to read out the cricket score from the local paper, just so he could hear him talk.
I don't know what's going on in his head. He's the one who explains thermodynamics to half our wing. After exams ended, the calls got shorter. Last week he told me, laughing, "I only called Papa once. He was offended." I think he's finding his feet.

qa.q: What did Madhav once ask his father to read out?
qa.a: The cricket score from the local paper.

qa.q: Why might Madhav ask his father not to cut the call during exams?
qa.a: Under exam stress and far from home, hearing Papa's voice seems to soothe him, the way a younger child needs comfort.

qa.q: What could Darshan do if Madhav's exam-time calls sound hard again?
qa.a: Offer company, like a study break or a walk, alongside the calls home, without teasing him about them.

qa.q: How might Madhav's father feel when the calls get shorter?
qa.a: Maybe a little left out, as his joking 'offence' shows, but also proud that Madhav is finding his feet. 🙂

grounding: A hostel neighbour hears a first-year student call his father daily and sound younger during exams, and notices the calls shrink as he settles.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
Week one of exams. Every night Farida sat on the hostel stairs with her phone, crying to her mother in Srinagar. "Mouji, just stay on the line while I revise." She asked her mother to tell her what she was cooking, again and again. Her roommate Nandini brought her tea and didn't ask any questions.
Week two. Farida still called, but mostly to read out flashcards while her mother said "hmm" and stirred the pot. The crying stopped halfway through the week.
Two months later. Farida called on a Sunday afternoon from the canteen, laughing. "Mouji, I topped the anatomy quiz!" Then she said, "I have to go, Nandini and I are going to the market." Her mother said, "Go, go," and sounded pleased.

qa.q: What did Farida ask her mother to do while she revised in week one?
qa.a: Just stay on the line.

qa.q: Why did Farida want her mother to keep telling her what she was cooking?
qa.a: Hearing ordinary home details made her feel close and looked after while she was stressed and far away.

qa.q: Which choice of Nandini's helped during week one, and why?
qa.a: Bringing tea without asking questions, which offered quiet company without making Farida feel judged for crying.

qa.q: How might Farida's mother have felt when Farida said, 'I have to go'?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved that her daughter sounded happy and settled, even if the calls were now shorter.

grounding: Over two months a first-year student moves from tearful nightly calls home during exams to short, cheerful ones as her confidence grows.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
"Payal, your mother says you've been calling every night from the hostel, crying. Your Indu Masi will tell you a secret.
When I went to Pune for nursing college at eighteen, I queued at the phone booth outside the hostel gate every single evening. I'd ask Baba to describe dinner, the dog, the mango tree, anything. During exams I talked to him like a little girl: 'Baba, tell me I'll pass. Say it again.' Once I cried so hard the booth man gave me a free sweet.
My roommate teased me. Baba never did. He said, 'Call as much as you need. You're not weak, you're far.'
By second year I was calling on Sundays. By third year, Baba complained I'd forgotten him.
So call, beta. You'll know when you need it less."

qa.q: Where did young Indu make her calls from?
qa.a: From the phone booth outside the hostel gate.

qa.q: Why did young Indu ask Baba to describe dinner, the dog and the mango tree?
qa.a: Hearing ordinary details from home comforted her when she felt far away and scared, especially during exams.

qa.q: What turned out to be the wisest part of Baba's response?
qa.a: He didn't tease her or push her to stop; saying "You're not weak, you're far" let her lean on him until her confidence grew.

qa.q: How might Payal feel hearing that Indu Masi once cried in a phone booth?
qa.a: Payal may feel less ashamed and less alone, seeing that someone in the family needed the same comfort and slowly grew out of it.

grounding: Shows, through an aunt's memory, a first-year student far from home who calls a parent daily and acts younger in exams, with comfort treated as a need that fades as confidence grows.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
The storm had knocked out the hostel Wi-Fi, and the only signal in Block D was on the terrace. So at ten, the night before his first thermodynamics exam, Baljeet, eighteen, stood under the water tank with the phone to his ear and rain blowing sideways.
"Mummy, tell me again how you make pinni. The whole way." His voice had gone small, the way it did when he was eight and had a fever. "And say I'll pass. Say it properly."
His roommate Kiran came up with an umbrella, held it over him without a word, then waited by the door.
Later, dripping, Baljeet muttered, "You must think I'm such a baby."
Kiran shrugged. "You're a whole country away from home in exam week. Makes sense."
After the last paper, Baljeet called home for five minutes, mostly to complain about the mess food.

qa.q: Where was the only signal in Block D?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet's voice go small on the call?
qa.a: Far from home with an exam the next day, Baljeet felt scared and needed comforting, so he slipped back into asking like the eight-year-old with a fever.

qa.q: What did Kiran's reply to "such a baby" get right?
qa.a: Kiran treated needing comfort as natural for someone far from home in exam week, not as weakness, so Baljeet could keep calling without shame 🙂

qa.q: What might Mummy feel, hearing Baljeet ask for the pinni recipe from a rainy terrace?
qa.a: Mummy may feel both touched and worried, glad to be the comfort Baljeet needs while missing having him close.

grounding: Illustrates a first-year student who, during exams and a storm, calls home and sounds younger than usual, with comfort treated as a need and the calls shrinking as the pressure passes.
